text: Yes. A woman is as much a person as any man, and the law should treat her so: the same vote, the same right to own property, sign contracts, serve on juries, and hold office. Customs that barred her were written by men for men; age alone doesn't make them just, and they have left countless women trapped and suffering.

Absolutely. Rights belong to persons, not to one sex. Women should vote, inherit, testify, stand for parliament, and keep their own wages on exactly the terms their brothers do. That clergy and old statute books once said otherwise proves only that they erred, and the error has cost women dearly in poverty and helplessness.

Yes, the very same rights men hold, without conditions. Denying women rights has meant beaten wives with no escape, mothers stripped of their children, girls married off against their will. Rights shouldn't have to be earned by proving usefulness or achievement; every woman is owed them simply as a human being. Traditions that sanctioned such suffering deserve no deference.

No. Scripture and the settled order of every Christian nation make the husband head of the household, and the realm is built of such households. Dragging women into the grime of electioneering would sully the modesty that keeps the home holy. Those who bear arms and toil for the country rightly govern it.

Certainly not. God made man and woman for different stations, and our fathers' wisdom has kept each in its place. A woman's honour lies in a chaste, sheltered life, not the corrupting clamour of the hustings. Men who defend the nation and provide for its families have earned the franchise; scattering it freely would unravel our people's order.

No. Heaven set the man over the woman as Christ over the Church, and a kingdom overturning that order invites chaos. Separate votes and estates for wives would pit them against husbands and split the family our community rests upon. Keeping women clear of politics' coarseness preserves their virtue; governing belongs to those who shoulder its burdens.

No. Political power should follow contribution. Men pay the bulk of taxes, serve in the militia, and bear the costs of war; those who carry the burdens of the state have earned the right to steer it. Women, who contribute differently, should not claim an identical share. Our constitution has long tied the franchise to such duties, and wisely.

Women who kept our munitions factories and hospitals running through the war have earned a voice in the nation they served. Let Parliament extend the franchise to them in orderly, lawful steps rather than yielding to street agitation, and let their votes help protect widows, children, and the working poor.

Not identical rights, no. Women and children need shielding from the harshness of factory, courtroom, and campaign, and laws that treat them just like men would strip away the protections that keep them from exploitation. Let husbands and fathers speak for their households as custom intends, and let women's gentler virtues stay unspoiled, safeguarding families and the community we share.

Our people cannot throw off foreign rule while half our strength sits idle. The movement needs its daughters as much as its sons, so let our national leaders write women's votes into the new constitution. Every household will then stand united behind the cause, and our mothers can guard our children's welfare against the occupier's laws.
